name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MATCHING_Q01 - Clinical and industrial applications of halogen compounds

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Compound) List-II (Application / Significance)
A. Chloramphenicol (i) Synthetic compound used for treatment of malaria
B. Thyroxine (ii) Volatile anaesthetic used during surgery
C. Halothane (iii) Chlorine-containing antibiotic used for treatment of typhoid fever
D. Chloroquine (iv) Iodine-containing hormone whose deficiency causes goiter

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Clinical role of Chloramphenicol
Chloramphenicol is a naturally occurring chlorine-containing broad-spectrum antibiotic produced by soil microorganisms, specifically prescribed for the clinical treatment of typhoid fever.

Step 2: Physiological role of Thyroxine
Thyroxine is an essential iodine-containing hormone secreted by the thyroid gland; inadequate dietary intake of iodine or deficiency of this hormone causes the metabolic disease known as goiter.

Step 3: Medical application of Halothane
Halothane (\(\mathrm{CF}_3\mathrm{CHBrCl}\)) is a synthetic polyhalogenated alkane widely utilized in modern medicine as a non-flammable inhalation general anaesthetic during surgical procedures.

Step 4: Therapeutic application of Chloroquine
Chloroquine is a synthetic halogen-containing pharmaceutical agent used worldwide for the prophylaxis and treatment of malaria.

Step 5: Conceptual matching conclusion
Pairing each substance with its primary physiological or medicinal property gives: Chloramphenicol — Chlorine-containing antibiotic used for treatment of typhoid fever; Thyroxine — Iodine-containing hormone whose deficiency causes goiter; Halothane — Volatile anaesthetic used during surgery; Chloroquine — Synthetic compound used for treatment of malaria. This establishes the sequence A-(iii), B-(iv), C-(ii), D-(i).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MATCHING_Q02 - Classification of halides based on carbon hybridisation

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Class of Halide) List-II (Defining Structural Characteristic)
A. Allylic halide (i) Halogen atom directly bonded to an \(sp^2\)-hybridised carbon of an aromatic ring
B. Vinylic halide (ii) Halogen atom bonded to an \(sp^3\)-hybridised carbon attached to an aromatic ring
C. Benzylic halide (iii) Halogen atom bonded to an \(sp^3\)-hybridised carbon adjacent to a carbon-carbon double bond
D. Aryl halide (iv) Halogen atom bonded to an \(sp^2\)-hybridised carbon of an aliphatic carbon-carbon double bond

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Classification of Allylic Halides
Allylic halides are compounds in which the halogen atom is bonded to an \(sp^3\)-hybridised carbon atom that is positioned immediately adjacent to an aliphatic carbon-carbon double bond (\(\mathrm{C=C}\)), termed an allylic carbon.

Step 2: Classification of Vinylic Halides
Vinylic halides are defined as compounds where the halogen atom is bonded directly to an \(sp^2\)-hybridised carbon atom constituting an aliphatic carbon-carbon double bond (\(\mathrm{C=C}\)).

Step 3: Classification of Benzylic Halides
Benzylic halides contain a halogen atom bonded to an \(sp^3\)-hybridised carbon atom that is directly attached to an aromatic ring (such as a benzene nucleus).

Step 4: Classification of Aryl Halides
Aryl halides (haloarenes) feature a halogen atom bonded directly to an \(sp^2\)-hybridised carbon atom belonging to an aromatic ring.

Step 5: Conceptual matching conclusion
Matching each class of halide with its defining structural characteristic establishes: Allylic halide — Halogen bonded to \(sp^3\) carbon adjacent to double bond; Vinylic halide — Halogen bonded to \(sp^2\) carbon of double bond; Benzylic halide — Halogen bonded to \(sp^3\) carbon attached to aromatic ring; Aryl halide — Halogen directly bonded to \(sp^2\) carbon of aromatic ring. This yields the sequence A-(iii), B-(iv), C-(ii), D-(i).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MATCHING_Q03 - Name reactions in haloalkane and haloarene synthesis

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Named Reaction) List-II (Reagent and Primary Synthetic Outcome)
A. Finkelstein reaction (i) Heating an alkyl chloride or bromide with a metallic fluoride like \(\mathrm{AgF}\) to yield an alkyl fluoride
B. Swarts reaction (ii) Treatment of a diazonium salt with cuprous chloride or bromide to replace the diazonium group
C. Wurtz reaction (iii) Reaction of an alkyl chloride or bromide with \(\mathrm{NaI}\) in dry acetone to yield an alkyl iodide
D. Sandmeyer reaction (iv) Treatment of alkyl halides with sodium in dry ether to yield a symmetrical alkane with doubled carbons

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Mechanism and transformation of the Finkelstein reaction
The Finkelstein reaction is a classical halogen exchange method in which alkyl chlorides or bromides react with sodium iodide (\(\mathrm{NaI}\)) dissolved in dry acetone. Precipitation of poorly soluble \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) or \(\mathrm{NaBr}\) in dry acetone drives the equilibrium forward by Le Chatelier's principle, synthesizing alkyl iodides (\(\mathrm{R-I}\)).

Step 2: Mechanism and transformation of the Swarts reaction
The Swarts reaction provides the standard route for the synthesis of alkyl fluorides (\(\mathrm{R-F}\)) by heating an alkyl chloride or bromide in the presence of heavy metallic fluorides, such as \(\mathrm{AgF}\), \(\mathrm{Hg}_2\mathrm{F}_2\), \(\mathrm{CoF}_2\), or \(\mathrm{SbF}_3\).

Step 3: Mechanism and transformation of the Wurtz reaction
In the Wurtz reaction, two molecules of alkyl halide are coupled by reaction with metallic sodium in anhydrous dry ether to generate higher symmetrical alkanes containing twice the carbon atoms of the initial halide.

Step 4: Mechanism and transformation of the Sandmeyer reaction
In the Sandmeyer reaction, freshly prepared arenediazonium salts undergo nucleophilic replacement of the diazo group (\(-\mathrm{N}_2^+\)) upon mixing with cuprous salts (\(\mathrm{Cu}_2\mathrm{Cl}_2\) or \(\mathrm{Cu}_2\mathrm{Br}_2\)), producing aryl chlorides or aryl bromides with the liberation of nitrogen gas.

Step 5: Conceptual matching conclusion
Correlating each reaction with its characteristic reagents and products gives: Finkelstein reaction — \(\mathrm{NaI}\) in dry acetone yielding alkyl iodide; Swarts reaction — Metallic fluorides yielding alkyl fluoride; Wurtz reaction — Sodium in dry ether yielding higher alkane; Sandmeyer reaction — Diazonium salt with cuprous halide yielding aryl halide. This matches the sequence A-(iii), B-(i), C-(iv), D-(ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MATCHING_Q04 - Ambident nucleophiles and nucleophilic substitution products

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Reagent reacting with \(\mathrm{R-X}\)) List-II (Major Substitution Product Class Formed)
A. \(\mathrm{KCN}\) (i) Nitroalkane (\(\mathrm{R-NO}_2\))
B. \(\mathrm{AgCN}\) (ii) Alkyl isocyanide (\(\mathrm{R-NC}\))
C. \(\mathrm{KNO}_2\) (iii) Alkyl nitrite (\(\mathrm{R-O-N=O}\))
D. \(\mathrm{AgNO}_2\) (iv) Alkyl cyanide / nitrile (\(\mathrm{R-CN}\))

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Behaviour of Potassium Cyanide (\(\mathrm{KCN}\))
Potassium cyanide is predominantly ionic in solution and dissociates completely into cyanide ions (\(:\!\mathrm{C}\equiv\mathrm{N}:^-\)). Although both carbon and nitrogen possess lone pairs capable of attack, the nucleophilic substitution occurs predominantly through the carbon atom because the formed carbon-carbon (\(\mathrm{C-C}\)) bond is thermodynamically much more stable than a carbon-nitrogen (\(\mathrm{C-N}\)) bond, yielding an alkyl cyanide (nitrile, \(\mathrm{R-CN}\)).

Step 2: Behaviour of Silver Cyanide (\(\mathrm{AgCN}\))
Silver cyanide is predominantly covalent in nature; the bond between silver and carbon is largely covalent, leaving the lone pair on the nitrogen atom freely available to initiate nucleophilic attack on the alkyl halide, resulting primarily in an alkyl isocyanide (\(\mathrm{R-NC}\)).

Step 3: Behaviour of Potassium Nitrite (\(\mathrm{KNO}_2\))
Potassium nitrite is an ionic salt providing ambident nitrite ions (\(^{-}\mathrm{O-N=O}\)). In solution, nucleophilic attack occurs through the oxygen atom possessing a formal negative charge, which forms an alkyl nitrite (\(\mathrm{R-O-N=O}\)) as the major product.

Step 4: Behaviour of Silver Nitrite (\(\mathrm{AgNO}_2\))
Silver nitrite possesses a predominantly covalent \(\mathrm{Ag-O}\) bond; consequently, the nitrogen atom donates its electron lone pair to attack the electrophilic carbon of the alkyl halide, yielding a nitroalkane (\(\mathrm{R-NO}_2\)) as the major product.

Step 5: Conceptual matching conclusion
Correlating each ambident reagent with its dominant substitution product class gives: \(\mathrm{KCN}\) — Alkyl cyanide (\(\mathrm{R-CN}\)); \(\mathrm{AgCN}\) — Alkyl isocyanide (\(\mathrm{R-NC}\)); \(\mathrm{KNO}_2\) — Alkyl nitrite (\(\mathrm{R-O-N=O}\)); \(\mathrm{AgNO}_2\) — Nitroalkane (\(\mathrm{R-NO}_2\)). This corresponds to the sequence A-(iv), B-(ii), C-(iii), D-(i).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MATCHING_Q05 - Environmental and health effects of polyhalogen compounds

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Polyhalogen Compound) List-II (Key Application / Physiological and Environmental Hazard)
A. Dichloromethane (\(\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{Cl}_2\)) (i) Historically used as an antiseptic due to the slow liberation of free iodine
B. Trichloromethane (\(\mathrm{CHCl}_3\)) (ii) Process solvent and paint remover that harms the central nervous system and impairs vision
C. Triiodomethane (\(\mathrm{CHI}_3\)) (iii) Industrial degreaser and fire extinguisher that causes ozone depletion and liver damage
D. Tetrachloromethane (\(\mathrm{CCl}_4\)) (iv) Precursor for Freon R-22 that oxidises slowly in light and air to form toxic phosgene gas

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Properties of Dichloromethane (\(\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{Cl}_2\))
Dichloromethane (methylene chloride) is widely employed as a paint remover, aerosol propellant, and solvent in the manufacture of pharmaceuticals. Exposure harms the human central nervous system, leading to impaired hearing, diminished vision, dizziness, and peripheral numbness.

Step 2: Properties of Trichloromethane (\(\mathrm{CHCl}_3\))
Trichloromethane (chloroform) is primarily used today in the industrial manufacturing of the refrigerant Freon R-22. In the presence of sunlight and atmospheric oxygen, it undergoes slow photo-oxidation to produce carbonyl chloride (\(\mathrm{COCl}_2\)), a deadly poisonous gas known as phosgene.

Step 3: Properties of Triiodomethane (\(\mathrm{CHI}_3\))
Triiodomethane (iodoform) was formerly used as an antiseptic. Its therapeutic antiseptic properties are not intrinsic to the \(\mathrm{CHI}_3\) molecule itself, but are entirely due to the slow liberation of elemental iodine upon application.

Step 4: Properties of Tetrachloromethane (\(\mathrm{CCl}_4\))
Tetrachloromethane (carbon tetrachloride) was extensively used as a cleaning agent, degreasing fluid, and fire extinguisher. When released into the atmosphere, it rises to the stratosphere where it depletes the protective ozone layer; chronic exposure causes liver cancer and severe neurological damage.

Step 5: Conceptual matching conclusion
Matching each polyhalogen compound with its primary hazard or role gives: Dichloromethane — Solvent and paint remover that harms the central nervous system; Trichloromethane — Precursor for Freon R-22 that oxidises to phosgene; Triiodomethane — Antiseptic acting via liberation of free iodine; Tetrachloromethane — Degreaser and fire extinguisher that causes ozone depletion. This establishes the sequence A-(ii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(iii).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MATCHING_Q06 - Basic terminology and principles of optical isomerism

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Stereochemical Concept) List-II (Precise Definition / Characteristic)
A. Chirality (i) An equimolar mixture of two enantiomers exhibiting zero net optical rotation
B. Enantiomers (ii) Preservation of the relative spatial arrangement of bonds to an asymmetric centre during a reaction
C. Racemic mixture (iii) Geometric property of an object or molecule that is non-superimposable on its mirror image
D. Retention of configuration (iv) Non-superimposable mirror-image stereoisomers that rotate plane-polarised light by equal magnitude in opposite directions

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Scientific definition of Chirality
Chirality is the geometric property of asymmetry displayed by an object or molecular structure that cannot be superimposed onto its own mirror image. Chiral molecules lack an internal plane or centre of symmetry and exhibit optical activity.

Step 2: Scientific definition of Enantiomers
Enantiomers are a pair of optical stereoisomers that are related as non-superimposable mirror images of one another. They possess identical chemical and physical properties in achiral environments but rotate plane-polarised light in equal magnitudes in opposite directions (dextrorotatory and laevorotatory).

Step 3: Scientific definition of a Racemic mixture
A racemic mixture (or racemic modification) contains equal proportions (50:50) of dextrorotatory and laevorotatory enantiomers. The optical rotation caused by molecules of one isomer is exactly compensated and cancelled by the opposite rotation of the other isomer, resulting in an optically inactive mixture designated as \((\pm)\) or \(dl\).

Step 4: Scientific definition of Retention of configuration
Retention of configuration describes a chemical reaction in which the relative three-dimensional spatial orientation of bonds at an asymmetric stereocentre remains completely preserved without inversion or change of absolute configuration.

Step 5: Conceptual matching conclusion
Aligning each term with its rigorous definition yields: Chirality — Property of non-superimposability on mirror image; Enantiomers — Non-superimposable mirror images rotating light in opposite directions; Racemic mixture — Equimolar mixture showing zero net optical rotation; Retention of configuration — Preservation of spatial arrangement of bonds to an asymmetric centre. This corresponds to the sequence A-(iii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MATCHING_Q07 - Electrophilic aromatic substitution reactions of chlorobenzene

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Reaction Conditions on Chlorobenzene) List-II (Major Organic Substitution Product)
A. \(\mathrm{Cl}_2\) in the presence of anhydrous \(\mathrm{FeCl}_3\) (i) 4-Chlorobenzenesulfonic acid
B. Concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\) + concentrated \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) (ii) 4-Chloroacetophenone
C. Heating with concentrated \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) (iii) 1,4-Dichlorobenzene
D. \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COCl}\) in the presence of anhydrous \(\mathrm{AlCl}_3\) (iv) 1-Chloro-4-nitrobenzene

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Directing influence in electrophilic substitution of chlorobenzene
The chlorine substituent on the benzene ring is weakly deactivating due to its strong \(-I\) (inductive) effect, but acts as an ortho-, para-directing group due to \(+R\) (resonance) electron donation that increases electron density predominantly at the ortho and para positions. Steric hindrance at the ortho position makes the symmetrical para-substituted product the predominant major product in all cases.

Step 2: Electrophilic chlorination of chlorobenzene
Treatment of chlorobenzene with chlorine gas in the presence of anhydrous \(\mathrm{FeCl}_3\) catalyst introduces an electrophilic chloronium ion, yielding 1,4-dichlorobenzene (para-isomer) as the major product alongside 1,2-dichlorobenzene (ortho-isomer) as the minor product.

Step 3: Electrophilic nitration of chlorobenzene
Reaction of chlorobenzene with nitrating mixture (concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO}_3\) and concentrated \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\)) produces the nitronium ion (\(\mathrm{NO}_2^+\)), which attacks preferentially to form 1-chloro-4-nitrobenzene as the major product.

Step 4: Electrophilic sulphonation of chlorobenzene
Heating chlorobenzene with concentrated sulphuric acid produces sulphur trioxide electrophile, yielding 4-chlorobenzenesulfonic acid as the major product.

Step 5: Friedel-Crafts acylation of chlorobenzene
Reaction of chlorobenzene with acetyl chloride (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COCl}\)) in the presence of anhydrous \(\mathrm{AlCl}_3\) Lewis acid generates the acylium electrophile (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{C}^+=\mathrm{O}\)), producing 4-chloroacetophenone as the major product.

Step 6: Conceptual matching conclusion
Matching each set of electrophilic conditions with the resulting major product gives: Chlorination — 1,4-Dichlorobenzene; Nitration — 1-Chloro-4-nitrobenzene; Sulphonation — 4-Chlorobenzenesulfonic acid; Friedel-Crafts acylation — 4-Chloroacetophenone. This establishes the sequence A-(iii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MATCHING_Q08 - Boiling point dipole moment and lattice symmetry trends

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Substance / Isomer) List-II (Characteristic Physical Trend / Experimental Property)
A. Chloromethane (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{Cl}\)) (i) Highest melting point among isomeric dihalobenzenes due to molecular symmetry and lattice fit
B. Iodomethane (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{I}\)) (ii) Lowest boiling point among isomeric bromobutanes due to spherical shape and minimal surface area
C. \(p\)-Dichlorobenzene (iii) Highest dipole moment among monohalomethanes (\(1.860\text{ D}\)) due to balance of charge and bond length
D. 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane (iv) Lowest \(\mathrm{C-X}\) bond enthalpy (\(234\text{ kJ/mol}\)) and highest boiling point among methyl halides

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Dipole moment of Chloromethane (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{Cl}\))
Dipole moment is the product of partial charge and bond distance (\(\mu = q \times d\)). Although fluorine is more electronegative than chlorine, the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond distance (\(178\text{ pm}\)) is significantly larger than the \(\mathrm{C-F}\) bond distance (\(139\text{ pm}\)). Consequently, chloromethane exhibits the highest dipole moment (\(1.860\text{ D}\)) among all halomethanes.

Step 2: Physical properties of Iodomethane (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{I}\))
Because the iodine atom has the largest atomic size and mass among the halogens, \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{I}\) experiences the strongest van der Waals dispersion forces, giving it the highest boiling point among the methyl halides. Concurrently, the greater bond length (\(214\text{ pm}\)) produces the lowest carbon-halogen bond dissociation enthalpy (\(234\text{ kJ/mol}\)).

Step 3: Melting point of \(p\)-Dichlorobenzene
While ortho-, meta-, and para-dichlorobenzene have very similar boiling points (\(453\text{ K}\), \(446\text{ K}\), and \(448\text{ K}\)), the melting point of the para-isomer (\(323\text{ K}\)) is substantially higher than the ortho- (\(256\text{ K}\)) and meta- (\(249\text{ K}\)) isomers. This is due to the high molecular symmetry of the para-isomer, which packs far more closely and securely into the crystal lattice.

Step 4: Boiling point of 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane
Among the constitutional isomers of bromobutane (\(\mathrm{C}_4\mathrm{H}_9\mathrm{Br}\)), branching increases from 1-bromobutane to 2-bromobutane to 2-bromo-2-methylpropane. Branching makes the molecule more spherical, diminishing surface contact area and lowering the magnitude of intermolecular van der Waals forces, which results in the lowest boiling point (\(346\text{ K}\)).

Step 5: Conceptual matching conclusion
Correlating each substance with its specific physical behavior establishes: Chloromethane — Highest dipole moment among monohalomethanes; Iodomethane — Lowest bond enthalpy and highest methyl halide boiling point; \(p\)-Dichlorobenzene — Highest melting point among dihalobenzenes due to crystal symmetry; 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane — Lowest boiling point among bromobutanes due to branching. This yields the sequence A-(iii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MATCHING_Q09 - Mechanistic and stereochemical pathways in substitution elimination

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Reaction / Transformation) List-II (Mechanistic Course and Stereochemical / Product Outcome)
A. \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction of an optically active secondary alkyl halide (i) Single-step concerted pathway yielding complete inversion of configuration
B. \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) reaction of an optically active secondary alkyl halide (ii) Requires drastic conditions (\(623\text{ K}\), \(300\text{ atm}\)) due to partial double-bond character of \(\mathrm{C-X}\)
C. Dehydrohalogenation of 2-bromopentane with alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\) (iii) Two-step pathway via a planar achiral carbocation leading to racemisation
D. Hydrolysis of chlorobenzene to phenol (iv) Governed by Zaitsev's rule yielding pent-2-ene as the major, more substituted alkene

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Mechanism of \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) substitution on chiral substrates
In an \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction, the rate-determining slow step generates an \(sp^2\)-hybridised carbocation intermediate that is trigonal planar and achiral. The incoming nucleophile attacks with equal probability from either side of the plane, giving equal amounts of retained and inverted products, which results in racemisation.

Step 2: Mechanism of \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) substitution on chiral substrates
An \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) reaction proceeds via a single-step concerted bimolecular mechanism where the nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbon from the rear (opposite to the departing halide). As the leaving group departs, the tetrahedral geometry flips like an umbrella in high wind, producing complete inversion of configuration (Walden inversion).

Step 3: Elimination pathway in 2-bromopentane
When 2-bromopentane is heated with alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\), it undergoes \(\beta\)-elimination of hydrogen and bromine. According to Zaitsev's (Saytzeff's) rule, the preferred alkene is that having the greater number of alkyl substituents on the double bond; hence, pent-2-ene is formed as the major product (\(81\%\)) while pent-1-ene is minor (\(19\%\)).

Step 4: Nucleophilic substitution of chlorobenzene
Chlorobenzene is exceptionally unreactive towards nucleophilic substitution compared to alkyl halides because resonance delocalisation gives the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond partial double-bond character (\(169\text{ pm}\) vs \(177\text{ pm}\)), and the \(sp^2\) carbon is more electronegative. Hence, conversion to phenol requires drastic industrial conditions (\(\mathrm{NaOH}\), \(623\text{ K}\), \(300\text{ atm}\)).

Step 5: Conceptual matching conclusion
Pairing each reaction with its characteristic mechanistic behaviour gives: \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) on chiral halide — Planar carbocation intermediate leading to racemisation; \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) on chiral halide — Concerted pathway giving inversion of configuration; Dehydrohalogenation of 2-bromopentane — Follows Zaitsev's rule to yield pent-2-ene; Hydrolysis of chlorobenzene — Requires drastic conditions due to partial double-bond character. This matches the sequence A-(iii), B-(i), C-(iv), D-(ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MATCHING_Q10 - Activating influence of nitro groups on haloarenes

questiontext.text:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Substrate undergoing Nucleophilic Hydroxylation) List-II (Specific Reaction Conditions for Phenol Formation)
A. Chlorobenzene (i) Aqueous \(\mathrm{NaOH}\), \(368\text{ K}\) followed by dilute \(\mathrm{H}^+\)
B. 1-Chloro-4-nitrobenzene (ii) Simply warming with water (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\))
C. 1-Chloro-2,4-dinitrobenzene (iii) Aqueous \(\mathrm{NaOH}\), \(623\text{ K}\), \(300\text{ atm}\) followed by dilute \(\mathrm{H}^+\)
D. 2,4,6-Trinitrochlorobenzene (iv) Aqueous \(\mathrm{NaOH}\), \(443\text{ K}\) followed by dilute \(\mathrm{H}^+\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Hydrolysis of unsubstituted Chlorobenzene
In chlorobenzene, nucleophilic attack of hydroxide ion is hindered by the electron-rich \(\pi\)-system and resonance stabilization of the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond. Conversion to phenol requires extremely harsh conditions: heating with aqueous sodium hydroxide at \(623\text{ K}\) under \(300\text{ atm}\) of pressure followed by acidification.

Step 2: Hydrolysis of 1-Chloro-4-nitrobenzene
The introduction of a strongly electron-withdrawing nitro group (\(-\mathrm{NO}_2\)) at the para-position stabilizes the developing negative charge on the Meisenheimer carbanionic intermediate through resonance. This facilitates nucleophilic substitution at a significantly milder temperature of \(443\text{ K}\) with aqueous \(\mathrm{NaOH}\).

Step 3: Hydrolysis of 1-Chloro-2,4-dinitrobenzene
With two strongly electron-withdrawing nitro groups located at both ortho and para positions relative to chlorine, the intermediate carbanion is delocalised and stabilised even further. As a consequence, substitution occurs smoothly at \(368\text{ K}\) in aqueous \(\mathrm{NaOH}\).

Step 4: Hydrolysis of 2,4,6-Trinitrochlorobenzene
When three nitro groups occupy all two ortho positions and the para position (2, 4, and 6), the benzene ring is intensely electron-deficient and the resulting carbanion intermediate is exceptionally stable. The chlorine atom is displaced simply by warming with water without requiring any added sodium hydroxide.

Step 5: Conceptual matching conclusion
Matching each nitro-substituted chlorobenzene derivative with the corresponding reaction conditions yields: Chlorobenzene — \(623\text{ K}\), \(300\text{ atm}\); 1-Chloro-4-nitrobenzene — \(443\text{ K}\); 1-Chloro-2,4-dinitrobenzene — \(368\text{ K}\); 2,4,6-Trinitrochlorobenzene — Simply warming with water. This establishes the sequence A-(iii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(ii).
